steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on using ChatGPT and street-level photographs to help enrich OpenStreetMap. It should give some background on generative AI and GeoAI, state our research questions, and explain why we use volunteered data sources.

steps.name: skeleton_outline

- GeoAI and LLMs in geospatial work; where our study fits

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Generative AI is a kind of AI that can make different types of content, like text, images, audio, code and simulations. It has gotten a huge amount of attention since ChatGPT was publicly released in late 2022. ChatGPT is a Large Language Model (LLM), which is a form of generative AI that produces language that sounds human-like. Since ChatGPT launched, researchers have been trying to understand what role AI could have for research, teaching and applications, and this includes the geographic information science (GIScience) community. ChatGPT can be used a lot for Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks, for example generating text, translating languages, writing software code and answering a plethora of questions, and this has both positive and adverse impacts. Generative AI has brought transformative opportunities for spatial data science. In this paper we look at whether generative AI can help human cartographers and GIS professionals to make the quality of maps better, and we use OSM as a test case (Figure 1).

GeoAI has been talked about in GIScience in recent years. For example, Janowicz et al. discussed whether it was possible to develop an artificial GIS analyst that can pass a domain specific Turing test. These questions are still mostly not answered, but using LLMs and foundational models in geospatial contexts goes in this direction. There are challenges because LLMs are trained in a different way than how humans learn spatial concepts, but these tools and methods are still being explored, for example to generate maps. Our study is also in this direction. We use an LLM (ChatGPT) and a multimodal pre-training method (BLIP-2) to connect visual and language information for mapping. We look at the larger question of whether generative AI is a useful tool for creating and enriching map databases, and more specifically we look at the following research questions:

- RQ1: natural language descriptions -> correct attribute tagging of road features?
- RQ2: can prompt engineering improve accuracy?
- RQ3: how much human analyst work can be substituted?

- VGI sources + off-the-shelf AI
  - fusion of freely available VGI (OSM, Mapillary) with off-the-shelf AI tools -> low-cost, uniformly available
  - OSM: collaborative, freely accessible worldwide map database (https://openstreetmap.org)
  - Mapillary: crowdsourced street-level photographs (https://mapillary.com); mapping, object detection, semantic segmentation, other computer vision
  - VGI not yet explored with generative AI; combining multiple VGI sources improves mapping
  - Mapillary images routinely used to enhance OSM

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Generative AI is a kind of AI that can make different types of content, like text, images, audio, code and simulations. It has gotten a huge amount of attention since ChatGPT was publicly released in late 2022. ChatGPT is a Large Language Model (LLM), which is a form of generative AI that produces language that sounds human-like. Since ChatGPT launched, researchers have been trying to understand what role AI could have for research, teaching and applications, and this includes the geographic information science (GIScience) community. ChatGPT can be used a lot for Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks, for example generating text, translating languages, writing software code and answering a plethora of questions, and this has both positive and adverse impacts. Generative AI has brought transformative opportunities for spatial data science. In this paper we look at whether generative AI can help human cartographers and GIS professionals to make the quality of maps better, and we use OSM as a test case (Figure 1).

GeoAI has been talked about in GIScience in recent years. For example, Janowicz et al. discussed whether it was possible to develop an artificial GIS analyst that can pass a domain specific Turing test. These questions are still mostly not answered, but using LLMs and foundational models in geospatial contexts goes in this direction. There are challenges because LLMs are trained in a different way than how humans learn spatial concepts, but these tools and methods are still being explored, for example to generate maps. Our study is also in this direction. We use an LLM (ChatGPT) and a multimodal pre-training method (BLIP-2) to connect visual and language information for mapping. We look at the larger question of whether generative AI is a useful tool for creating and enriching map databases, and more specifically we look at the following research questions:

- 1. Can generative AI turn natural language text descriptions into the correct attribute tagging of road features in digital maps?

- 2. For this problem, can the accuracy of the suggestions be improved with prompt engineering?

- 3. How much of the work of human analysts can be substituted with generative AI approaches in these kinds of mapping processes?

Also, our approach focuses on combining freely available volunteered geographic information (VGI) data sources (OSM, Mapillary) and off-the-shelf AI tools, so the solution can be low-cost and uniformly available. OSM is a collaborative project that wants to create a freely accessible worldwide map database (https://openstreetmap.org). Mapillary crowdsources street-level photographs (https://mapillary.com) which are used for mapping and other applications, such as object detection, semantic segmentation and other computer vision algorithms that extract semantic information from imagery. VGI has not been explored yet together with generative AI, but previous studies showed that it is practical to combine multiple sources of VGI to improve the mapping process. More specifically, Mapillary street-level images are routinely used to enhance OSM.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is a type of AI that can produce various types of content, including text, images, audio, code, and simulations. It has gained enormous attention since ChatGPT was publicly released in late 2022. ChatGPT is an example of a Large Language Model (LLM), a form of generative AI that produces human-like language. Since the launch of ChatGPT, researchers, including the geographic information science (GIScience) community, have been trying to understand the potential role of AI for research, teaching, and applications. ChatGPT can be used extensively for Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks such as text generation, language translation, writing software code, and generating answers to a plethora of questions, with both positive and adverse impacts [1]. The emergence of generative AI has introduced transformative opportunities for spatial data science. In this paper, we explore the potential of generative AI to help human cartographers and GIS professionals increase the quality of maps, using OSM as a test case (Figure 1).

GeoAI has been part of the GIScience discourse in recent years. For example, Janowicz et al. [2] elaborated on whether it was possible to develop an artificial GIS analyst that passes a domain specific Turing test. Although these questions are still largely unanswered, using LLMs and foundational models in geospatial contexts contributes to this direction. Despite the challenges arising from the different nature of LLM training methodologies and human learning of spatial concepts [3], these tools and methods are being explored, for example to generate maps [4]. Our study fits into this direction by using an LLM (ChatGPT) and a multimodal pre-training method (BLIP-2) to connect visual and language information in the context of mapping. We explore the larger question of whether generative AI is a useful tool for creating and enriching map databases and more specifically investigate the following research questions:

- 1. Is generative AI capable of turning natural language text descriptions into the correct attribute tagging of road features in digital maps?

- 2. For this problem, can the accuracy of suggestions be improved through prompt engineering [5]?

- 3. To what extent can the work of human analysts be substituted with generative AI approaches within these mapping processes?

Furthermore, our approach focuses on the fusion of freely available volunteered geographic information (VGI) [6] data sources (OSM, Mapillary) and off-the-shelf AI tools to present a potentially low-cost and uniformly available solution. OSM is a collaborative project that aims to create a freely accessible worldwide map database (https://openstreetmap.org), while Mapillary crowdsources street-level photographs (https://mapillary.com) that power mapping and other applications, such as object detection, semantic segmentation and other computer vision algorithms that extract semantic information from imagery [7]. While VGI has not yet been explored in the context of generative AI, previous studies demonstrated that combining multiple sources of VGI to improve the mapping process is practicable [8]. In particular, Mapillary street-level images are routinely used to enhance OSM [9,10].
